Food Delivery App (Zomato/Swiggy) — LLD

A good interview-level design should cover:

User places order
Restaurant manages menu
Delivery partner assigned
Order tracking
Payment
Order states
Basic scalability/extensibility

This problem is mainly based on:

Strategy Pattern → delivery assignment, pricing
State Pattern → order lifecycle
Observer Pattern → live tracking/notifications
Singleton → services/managers
Factory (optional) → payment creation


Core Requirements
Functional Requirements

Customer
    Browse restaurants
    View menu
    Add items to cart
    Place order
    Pay
    Track order

Restaurant
    Manage menu
    Accept/reject order
    Prepare food

Delivery Partner
    Accept delivery
    Pick order
    Deliver order

    Game

🧪 Follow-up Questions (Microsoft LOVES these)

    1️⃣ How would you add Check / Checkmate?
        Add isKingInCheck(Board, Player)
        Simulate move → validate king safety
    
    2️⃣ How to support Castling / En Passant?
        Extend Move with metadata
        Add rule engines per move type
    
    3️⃣ How to make it thread-safe?
        Synchronize makeMove
        Or single-threaded game loop
    
    4️⃣ How to persist game state?
        Serialize Board
        Store moves as events (event sourcing)

Key UML Relationships (Important to Explain in Interview)
1️⃣ Composition
    GameService owns UserProgress
    Lifecycle tied to the game session
2️⃣ Interface-based polymorphism
    GameService → GuessEvaluator
    GameService → GameRules
This allows:
Different evaluation logic
Different rule sets (easy / hard mode)

3️⃣ No circular dependencies
    All arrows point towards abstractions
    Concrete classes sit at the edges
This is a big Microsoft design plus.

Job Posting Service – LLD (Microsoft SDE-2)

1. Requirements (Clarified in Interview Style)

Functional
    Recruiter can post a job
    Candidate can apply to a job
    Maintain candidate profile (skills, YOE)
    Recruiter sees top matching candidates for a job
    Candidate sees top eligible jobs
    Matching logic is the core

Non-Functional (Lightweight)
    In-memory (no DB)
    Read-heavy
    Deterministic ranking
    Easy to extend (weights, filters)

2. Core Design Decisions (Checklist Friendly)

   | Area      | Decision            | Why MS Likes It      |
   | --------- | ------------------- | -------------------- |
   | Pattern   | Strategy (Matching) | Extensible scoring   |
   | Storage   | In-memory Maps      | Interview-friendly   |
   | Ranking   | Score-based         | Clear logic          |
   | Threading | Single-thread       | Explicitly stated    |
   | APIs      | Service layer       | Clean separation     |
   | Code      | Fully runnable      | Explicit requirement |

3.Data Models

Candidate
Job


4. Matching Strategy (Most Important)

Scoring Rules (Explain Verbally)
  -  Skill match → 70% weight
  - Experience match → 30% weight
  - Candidate must satisfy minimum experience

1. Understand + Clarify + Scope
    What are the core features? (must-have vs good-to-have)
    What scale? (single machine vs distributed)
    Any constraints? (concurrency, latency, memory)

Example:
Ride sharing:
    Book ride? ✅
    Match driver? ✅
    Payment? ❌ (skip)

--------------------------------------------------------------

2. IDENTIFY CORE ENTITIES (MOST IMPORTANT STEP)
Trick: Extract all nouns from problem statement

Example:
🚕 Ride Sharing
    User
    Driver
    Ride
    Location
    MatchingService

🎬 BookMyShow
    User
    Movie
    Show
    Seat
    Booking

💰 Splitwise
    User
    Expense
    Group
    Balance

Golden Rule:  If it has state + behavior → make it a class

--------------------------------------------------------------
🧱 3. CLASSIFY ENTITIES (Pattern Recognition)

Every LLD problem fits into these buckets:

    1. Core Entities (data holders)
    User
    Ride
    Seat
    Item 

    2. Manager / Service Classes (brain)
        RideManager
        BookingService
        ExpenseManager

    These handle:
    business logic
    orchestration

    3. Strategy / Policy Classes (optional)
    PricingStrategy
    MatchingStrategy
    PaymentStrategy

--------------------------------------------------------------

4. DEFINE RELATIONSHIPS
Ask:
    One-to-one?
    One-to-many?
    Many-to-many?

Example:
    One User → Many Rides
    One Show → Many Seats

--------------------------------------------------------------

5. WRITE INTERFACE / FLOW FIRST (VERY IMPORTANT)

Before coding classes, define flow:

Example (Ride booking)
    User → requestRide()
    RideManager → findDriver()
    Driver → acceptRide()
    Ride → start()
    Ride → end()

--------------------------------------------------------------

6.PICK DESIGN PATTERNS (IF NEEDED)

| Pattern   | When to use                             |
| --------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Singleton | One manager (RideManager)               |
| Strategy  | Multiple algorithms (pricing, matching) |
| Observer  | Notifications                           |
| State     | Vending machine, order state            |
| Factory   | Object creation                         |


--------------------------------------------------------------

7. START CODING (STRUCTURED WAY)

Order matters 

    Step 1: Enums
        enum RideStatus { REQUESTED, ONGOING, COMPLETED };
    Step 2: Core Classes
        class User {};
        class Driver {};
        class Ride {};
    Step 3: Manager Classes
        class RideManager {};
    Step 4: Glue everything



input -> manager (should have methods like init,book,.... and will have unorderedmap or vector for multiple games/rides etc/)
-> manager.x to entity.x (entity is reponsible for updating)

Use #include<bits/stdc++.h>
Use Initializer list for members initialization, refer Initializer_List.cpp
use unique_ptr, and shared_ptr in runtime creation

Mistakes:
access modifier , change to public for methods:
call methods of pointer instances using ->
call methods of stack instances using .
close the class in cpp with ;

    3. Classify:

Multithreading Tools in C++

-----------------------------------------------------------
| Feature                   | Use                         |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `std::thread`             | Create threads              |
| `std::mutex`              | Protect shared data         |
| `std::lock_guard`         | Safe mutex handling         |
| `std::condition_variable` | Thread communication        |
| `std::future`             | Async result                |
| `std::async`              | Automatic thread management |
| `std::atomic`             | Lock-free variables         |
------------------------------------------------------------


When to Use Which
-------------------------------------------------------
| Tool                 | Use Case                     |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `mutex + lock_guard` | protect complex shared data  |
| `condition_variable` | threads waiting for an event |
| `atomic`             | simple counters / flags      |
-------------------------------------------------------


If you're doing C++ LLD interviews, the 3 most common concurrency patterns you’ll see are:
   1. Thread-safe cache (mutex)
   2. Producer–Consumer queue (condition_variable)
   3. Rate limiter counters (atomic)
Learning these three covers almost all interview scenarios.

We can use different Pointer Patterns in different use case but generally we avoid using raw pointers in interviews

There can be 5 patterns, we can use while working with instances:
1.) Unique pointer 
2.) Shared pointer (most prefered)
3.) Weak pointer (very less frequently use)
4.) Raw Pointers (creating instances on runtime) (never use in interviews)
5.) Stack based (For managers, when other classes uses it, but doesn't own it) 


1. unique_ptr → Ownership
    Use unique_ptr when only one class owns the object.

Meaning:
    No other class should share it

When the owner dies → object dies

Use Case :  generally creating something on main function like Board, Manager, etc... we can either use unique_ptr 
            or even references

Example :
Car → Engine
Board → Dice
House → Rooms
Order → OrderItems


2. shared_ptr → Shared Ownership (Most Preferred, as it provides flexibility to use the same instance at multiple places)
Use shared_ptr when multiple objects share the same instance. 
Example: Players using same game board

Use shared_ptr when:
    multiple objects need same resource

Examples:
    Players → Board
    Subscribers → Channel
    Services → Strategy
    Users → Logger


3. Raw Pointer → Non Ownership
Use raw pointer when class does NOT own the object.

Use raw pointer when:
    reference only
    no ownership

Examples:
    Command → Receiver
    Iterator → Container
    Strategy → Context


4. weak_ptr → Avoid Circular Dependency (Rarely needed)
Used with shared_ptr. 

A → shared_ptr → B
B → shared_ptr → A



Follow this approach:
stack → reference → unique_ptr → shared_ptr → raw pointer

🔥 MOST COMMON FOLLOW-UPS (and How to Answer)
1“What happens if many expired entries exist but cache is full?”

Expected answer:
We can lazily clean expired entries during put() or periodically via a background cleanup thread.

If pushed:
On put(), walk from tail and remove expired nodes
Or run a scheduled cleaner

2 “How would you improve scalability?”

Say:
Current solution uses a single lock
For higher throughput:
Segment the cache
One lock per segment
Similar to ConcurrentHashMap design

This answer is enough — no need to code it.
3. “Why not use LinkedHashMap?”

Perfect answer:
LinkedHashMap doesn’t support TTL and fine-grained eviction control.
Writing it manually gives extensibility and control.

4.“What is the complexity if cleanup runs?”

Answer:
Normal ops → O(1)
Cleanup → O(n) worst case, but amortized cost is acceptable


5.“What if capacity is very large?”

Say:
Memory bound
Can store values off-heap or spill to disk (out of scope for LLD)

6.“What if TTL is very small?”

Answer:
Lazy eviction avoids extra threads
High churn but correctness maintained

7️⃣ “How would you make it distributed?”

Correct response:

That moves into system design, not LLD.
We’d need sharding, consistent hashing, and distributed eviction.

Important:
Don’t over-design here.

⚠️ TRICK QUESTIONS THEY SOMETIMES ASK
❓ “Is this deadlock-free?”
✔ Yes — single lock, no nested locks

❓ “Can this starve threads?”

✔ Minimal risk; lock scope is small

❓ “What happens if ttlMillis is zero or negative?”

✔ Entry expires immediately — acceptable or can guard input

🚫 Things That WOULD FAIL You

❌ Pseudocode only
❌ Using LinkedHashMap directly
❌ No locking discussion
❌ Over-engineering with executors, timers, etc.
